abstract: Pacific salmon hold high ecological, cultural, and economical importance, but climate change is constraining their survival and reproductive success. Warming rivers are one of the foremost threats, with many populations increasingly facing temperatures approaching or exceeding their physiological limits. Understanding and predicting these negative impacts can inform mitigation or offsetting measures. We used a 12-year dataset of 13801 individually-tagged fish to develop a detailed model of Okanagan sockeye salmon migration based on functional relationships with river temperature and flow. Okanagan sockeye are the largest of the last two self-sustaining sockeye populations in the Columbia River basin. Their abundance increased dramatically over the last two decades amid significant rehabilitation efforts. However, Okanagan sockeye migrate into one of the species' warmest inhabited regions in North America and are highly vulnerable to climate change. Our model revealed temperature thresholds associated with migration cessation and mortality near 21{degrees}C and 25{degrees}C, respectively. These temperatures are common during the migration period in the Okanogan River, which sockeye must ascend to reach the spawning grounds. We used the estimated functional relationships to parameterize forward simulations of Okanagan sockeye migration from 2006-2025, spanning all years where water and fish passage data were available. These simulations accurately predicted migration timing and survival through the Okanogan River, providing a forecasting tool for Canadian fishery managers to regulate harvest in Osoyoos Lake. The simulations also showed elevated mortality rates during warm years and highlighted the perils associated with brief periods of river cooling, which apparently trigger large influxes of salmon migrants who may subsequently be exposed to extreme temperatures and experience high mortality rates. Our work highlights the potential for functional models to provide detailed and accurate reconstructions and forecasts of Pacific salmon migration success, which managers will require as river temperatures increasingly exceed salmon physiological limits.
